description: Hello! I'm Emilio, into computer vision and creating immersive experiences. I can help with web development (GSAP, CSS, Tailwind, Three.js), coming up with ideas, and project planning. I'd love to meet people who have ideas of their own and want to build something cool together. If you're looking to try things out, make new connections, and learn along the way, come join :) We can work in English or Spanish.
summary:
Musica Universalis is an educational website that transforms NASA’s aerosol visualization into an interactive and immersive musical experience. Developed for the Earth Jukebox challenge, it introduces dust, sea salt, smoke, and sulfates through distinct musical voices.

The website offers three connected experiences. First, a guided introduction explains aerosols and helps visitors recognize their sounds and spatial positions. Next, visitors listen to a concert generated as the application reads the map from left to right, translating its visual patterns into a musical sequence. Finally, an exploration mode lets visitors move freely across the map and hear how the music changes between locations.

Sound responds in real time to pixel intensity, the prevalence of aerosol-associated colors, and the dominant color within each area. Particularly strong patterns trigger additional melodies. These sounds interpret the visualization rather than directly measuring aerosol concentrations.

Designed with blind and low-vision users in mind, Musica Universalis combines spoken guidance, scientific education, and musical exploration to broaden access to atmospheric information and invite people to discover Earth through listening.
details:
Musica Universalis is an educational website that helps people explore Earth’s atmosphere through listening. Developed for the Earth Jukebox challenge, it transforms NASA’s aerosol visualization into music, offering another way to engage with information usually communicated visually. It is designed with blind and low-vision users in mind, while also welcoming visitors without a scientific background.

The experience follows a progression from learning to independent discovery. Visitors first learn about aerosols and recognize their musical voices. They then hear those voices combined in a concert generated as the application reads the map from left to right. Finally, they explore freely, choosing locations and listening to how the music changes. This progression gives visitors a sound vocabulary they can use to interpret the map themselves.

Python scripts preprocess the visualization into aerosol-associated color masks and a JSON spatial mapping. During playback, JavaScript uses this information while Tone.js synthesizes and schedules the music. Pixel intensity, color prevalence, and dominant patterns influence the composition, with particularly strong patterns triggering additional melodies. Sea salt becomes a sustained synthesizer pad, dust a rhythmic arpeggio, sulfates bright bells, and smoke a low bass. These sounds interpret image patterns rather than directly measuring aerosol concentrations.

The creative foundation comes from the Pythagorean “harmony of the spheres,” which connects music, mathematical proportions, and the cosmos. The musical system transposes one cycle per Earth year upward by 32 octaves to approximately 136.10 Hz, then builds a just-intonation pentatonic scale using simple frequency ratios. This provides a coherent musical framework within which visitors shape their own listening journeys.

I developed the project independently using HTML, JavaScript, Python, JSON, and Tone.js. ElevenLabs provided the narrations. Claude supported algorithm development and image-complexity mapping, while ChatGPT assisted with visual design and debugging.

Accessibility, storytelling, scientific clarity, and performance guided the design. Spoken instructions explain both the science and the interaction. Screen-reader accessibility was considered, although compatibility has not been formally verified. Choosing a still image instead of video kept the prototype manageable, while preprocessing moved image analysis out of interactive playback so more computational resources could support audio generation.

The intended impact is to make atmospheric science more approachable and encourage curiosity about the environment. By connecting explanation, musical interpretation, and personal exploration, Musica Universalis invites more people to discover the patterns and beauty of Earth’s atmosphere.
